The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Inside the themed chassis, you get 256GB of built-in storage (expandable with microSD Express cards), a vivid display in handheld mode, faster load times, and support for up to 4K resolution on compatible TVs when the console sits in the dock.

The magnetic Joy-Con 2 controllers add mouse-style tracking in supported games, while the newly introduced GameChat hub lets you voice chat and share your screen directly as you play. It also plays your older Switch games and supports standard multiplayer options.

Landing limited-edition Nintendo hardware takes a little prep work, but these battle-tested habits will give you a real edge over the bots:.

Recent findings suggest that hands off the refresh button in Best Buy's queue — When an online drop goes live, Best Buy puts shoppers into a randomized waiting line to filter out scrapers. Touching the reload button resets your spot and boots you straight to the back.

In a recent development, watch for Walmart+ early-access paywalls — Walmart frequently locks headline console drops behind paid Walmart+ subscriptions for the first 30 to 60 minutes. If you have a membership, keep that tab signed in; if not, wait for the general public window to unlock.

According to recent reports, dodge third-party sellers — Double-check the seller before buying. Marketplace scalpers frequently list units for jacked-up prices; make sure it notes "Sold and shipped by [Retailer]" at the standard price.

Skip the web wars and head to physical stores — Online checkout bots grab website stock in under 15 seconds. Showing up in person is easily your most reliable path to securing one without paying scalper markups.

Stores like Walmart, Amazon, and Best Buy often hold onto popular gaming hardware to use as headline deals during Black Friday and Cyber Monday week.

With that stated, Black Friday restocks are usually the hardest ones to catch. You will be fighting website crashes, gift shoppers, and automated bots all at once. If you can grab a console whenever stock appears, take it. Think of Black Friday as a backup initiative, not your main bet.

Console hunting sucks right now, period. But between the surprise micro-drops and physical store restocks, you still have real shots at retail price — just be ready to move the second that stock goes live.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Wallet for Android is rolling out support for digital home keys if you have a compatible smart lock in Google Home.

After adding a home key to Google Wallet, you can Tap to Unlock with your phone. This leverages NFC and “works even when your phone screen is locked” by default. However, you can adjust verification settings in the Google Wallet app to require screen lock or biometric authentication. This requires Android 9+.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also support for Unlock on Approach with an Aliro Ultra Wideband (UWB)-compatible Android phone (see below) and an Aliro UWB-compatible lock. Wear OS watches are not supported at launch.

Behind the scenes, the digital key is linked to the Google Home app rather than a single lock. As such, “each of your compatible Aliro locks will work with a single key in your Google Wallet.” Keys are added to Google Wallet using the Home app, which will prompt you to save after setup. You can also go to Home settings > Google Wallet key.

Recent findings suggest that crazy to me that Google's own smart lock with Yale doesn't have this functionality. Seems like a huge miss for them to not be forward looking with their own hardware here.

Afterward, your key “automatically syncs across compatible Android phones signed into your Google Wallet account.”.

The card in Google Wallet features a simple Google Home logo with your home’s name in the top-right corner.

Sources indicate that the following locks are supported at launch: Aqara u400 (UWB and NFC), Schlage Sense Pro (NFC at launch and UWB to follow), and Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Support for more models is coming.

Additionally, support is rolling out first to the Google Home Public Preview before coming to all users “over the coming weeks.”.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang’s midlife-crisis makeover hasn’t helped the Nvidia CEO’s image this week.
  • As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.
  • This is where WIRED comes to the rescue, aided by Vogue, GQ and a celebrity stylist, no less.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s midlife-crisis makeover hasn’t helped the Nvidia CEO’s image this week. In a matter of days, Huang’s questionable sartorial leanings have shifted wildly from wannabe cool Harley dad to low-down leather Lothario. Fashion moves fast, but even in the style world, this is a breakneck volte-face.

As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.

This is where WIRED comes to the rescue, aided by Vogue, GQ and a celebrity stylist, no less. We’ve charted the menacing glow-up of tech bros before, but merely observing the worrying trend back in 2025 is clearly no longer enough. It’s time to roll up our Armani sleeves and help.

It has been revealed that “Tech bros were total nerds before," notes Karen Clarkson, a professional stylist whose clients have included Nike, Google, Apple, Calvin Klein, and Vivienne Westwood. "Fashion didn’t touch their lives at all. They didn’t have style.” Pictures of Huang’s pre-biker fashion-vacuum days certainly bear this out. “Then, like [Jeff] Bezos, they all stepped up. And there’s a rivalry that’s come with that, whether it’s the fashion makeover, the grooming, the skin treatments, or gym regimen. Now we have Mark Zuckerberg in the front row at Prada.”.

Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 1! (clockwise from top left): Giorgio Armani long-sleeved cashmere polo, $1,695; Lemaire workwear jacket, $1,050; The Row Nesper pant, $1,250; Giorgio Armani leather slippers, $1,850; Speciale cotton-mix stripe shirt; £295.

According to recent reports, as a man clearly in dress distress, where better to start than with Murray Clark, head of editorial at British GQ. Controversially, Clark has a radical notion that Huang should keep clothing matters as they are. “I’d argue that Jensen Huang stays exactly how he is because this is who he is—a coiffed, leather-jacket wearing, mistake-making middle-aged man for all the world to see.”.

Before publicly admitting on Sunday to having an affair with a businesswoman who US intelligence states is also a Chinese spy, in 2024, Huang confessed onstage that his wife, Lori, suggested and chose his biker outfits for him because he found most other fabrics “itchy.”.

According to recent reports, if Jensen keeps his jackets (he apparently owns 30 to 40), Clarkson thinks that Huang might even find himself on the catwalk. “If he wants to go down that route, then for sure Demna [Gucci’s creative director] would have him walking in his next show in Milan,” she indicates. “But he’s very Arnold Schwarzenegger and the Terminator with his black leathers, which is a bit close to the bone, really, with AI and that humanity is potentially doomed. I don’t know if he’s wise to lean into Arnie too heavily.”.

Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 2! (clockwise from top left): The Row Vana jacket, $12,000; Speciale lambswool crew, £435; The Row Victor shirt, $1,290; Lemaire Rail Belt, $320; John Lobb City II New Standard shoes, $1,878; The Row Paulo corduroy pant, $1,590.

In a recent development, let’s get some sage advice, then, from Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial at British Vogue. “If I were styling Jensen Huang, I’d advise him to cleanse the palate entirely, ditch the rock and roll shrunken leather jackets for something more somber,” Nnadi claims. “A collared Oxford shirt and a navy or gray crewneck jumper would do the trick and wouldn’t read as aggressively corporate as a traditional suit. The message needs to be ‘I’m a serious person, and I’m leaving that tragic try-hard boomer dad wardrobe behind along with my despicable behavior.’”.

Industry observers note that clarkson agrees, saying that while the term “unapologetic” is often used in fashion, in this instance, Huang needs a more apologetic dress code, moving away from anything too flashy. So out go the overtly sexual Tom Ford leathers—which Jensen can handily sell off for $1 million a pop to his Huang-boys to offset any alimony outlays that may, or may not, be coming his way—and in come understated and neutral tones.

“He could take a leaf out of Harry Styles’ dress down codes and check The Row for minimal looks,” Clarkson claims. “A Lemaire workwear jacket is also a good vibe. It shows he’s willing to put in the work to win back his family. Also, since he’s spoken about feeling itchy, maybe he should repent a bit and wear lambswool instead of cashmere.”.

Industry observers note that jensen Huang's Banished Biker Look 3! (clockwise from top left): Paul Smith Ripstop field jacket, $1,025; Brunello Cucinelli alpaca-blend sweater, $3,400; The Row Sue pant, $2,300; Paul Smith Garson shoes, $475.

Asking Clarkson to step away from her celebrity clients for a moment to perform a hasty hypothetical make under (or glow down?) for Huang, she has very kindly put together three outfits that I think we can all agree give off considerably fewer bad-egg biker vibes with pieces from Paul Smith, The Row, Lemaire, Giorgio Armani, Brunello Cucinelli, and more. If you’re lucky enough to have a budget to match Huang's, we’ve added links to the individual pieces in the captions under each “look.”.

“There’s been a lot of tight-fitted leather jackets that just about cover his biceps, which always feels like he’s looking to lure his next lover or like he’s just whizzed off on his Ducati to have a quick lunchtime visit with his mistress,” says Clarkson. “That’s not the vibe you want to go before Congress with.” For the Hill, she suggests Huang go for a Nehru collar that “feels a bit more buttoned up.”.

Giorgio Armani's Spring-Summer 2027 show in Milan.

Recent findings suggest that however, because Huang’s existing look is so strong, Clarkson advises that changing it too quickly will not only draw an enormous amount of commentary but even more memes. “Little steps, not a full overnight makeover. That’s why he should perhaps keep the leather jacket, something like a suede blouson instead of the biker,” she says, adding that the black jeans should be ditched in favor of proper pants.

“He could do a tie as well—a bit more apologetic, a bit more formal, a bit more respectful. So a brown leather jacket with a tie and a shirt—so then it’s a segue into a new direction,” Clarkson indicates, citing Giorgio Armani’s June Milan collection as ideal inspiration.

However, Clarkson states credit must ultimately go to Lori Huang, Jensen’s wife of 41 years. “She did a brilliant job. If anyone comes out of this as a winner, it’s her. She could rebrand as a Hollywood stylist at this point because she’s done a great job of creating an identity for her husband. Almost too good because it’s attracted too many women. Still, she could step away with a really great divorce settlement and a whole new career.”.

True to the collection's signature design quirks, the builds repurpose familiar Lego elements in clever ways, such as bright green dinosaur eggs posing as budding peonies and minifigure crowns serving as cherry blossom centers.

In a recent development, three of the sets arrive on Upcoming Year's Day, while the pastel bouquet lands just in time for Valentine's Day. Here's a closer look at each new build coming to the garden:.

According to recent reports, unlike most flower builds that require you to find a spare jar or vase around the house, the Lego Botanicals Cherry Blossom Branches comes as an all-in-one display unit. The 405-piece build features realistic branches packed with white sakura petals and pale pink buds, all seated directly inside an ocean-blue brick-built vase. It also carries Lego’s signature design quirks, repurposing minifigure crowns in fresh colorways to build the buds and flower centers.

Measuring over 8 inches tall, 7 inches wide, and 5.5 inches deep, it hits a rare sweet spot for home decor: compact enough to fit neatly on a crowded bookshelf or work desk without dominating the whole surface.

Sources indicate that most Lego botanical sets recreate garden-variety stems, but the Lego Botanicals Wild Orchid tackles one of the most distinctive, hard-to-grow plants in nature: the rare blue Vanda coerulea. The 606-piece build stands over 11.5 inches tall, 13 inches wide, and 4.5 inches deep, functioning as a complete self-contained forest ecosystem rather than just loose flowers.

Instead of sitting in a traditional pot, the vibrant blue blossoms and aerial roots sprout directly from a textured, mossy branch accented with miniature wildlife. Lego introduced newly introduced printed petal elements specifically for this release to mirror the natural veining and delicate look of real orchid petals. You can reposition the stems and flowers to customize the shape, giving you an eye-catching tabletop centerpiece that captures the detail of a live botanical display.

It has been revealed that peonies are notorious for shedding petals and drooping within a few days of bringing them home, but the Lego Botanicals Peony Bouquet gives you the full, layered look without the short lifespan. The 633-piece set features a mix of single blooms, semi-double flowers, and buds at different stages of opening, blending shades of ombré peach, pale pink, and deep pink with bright yellow stamens.

In classic Lego fashion, the designer's use of parts steals the show: bright green dinosaur eggs are repurposed along the branches to recreate rounded peony buds about to open. With the longest stem measuring over 16.5 inches, the entire arrangement fits in standard household vases without extra props.

If you already own a vase and want a wide variety of stems to arrange yourself, the Lego Botanicals Perfectly Pastel Flower Bouquet delivers the most diverse floral mix in the entire 2027 drop. The 650-piece set includes 16 individual stems spanning eight different varieties: three hybrid tea roses, three coneflowers, two columbines, two anemones, two pincushion flowers, a stock flower, phlox, and sword ferns.

Sources indicate that lego kept the color palette soft with muted pastel tones, but hid a neat Easter egg inside: a tiny Lego beehive element tucked directly into the cone of one of the flowers. Measuring over 15 inches tall, the stems are fully adjustable, so you can lengthen, shorten, or reposition each blossom to suit different vase heights or mix them with earlier Lego bouquets for an even fuller display.

Between Upcoming Year's Day shelf refreshes and early Valentine's Day shopping, you can shop all four upcoming arrangements on Lego.

Samsung and Google are finally launching their Android XR smart glasses, as previously reported. The first collection pairs Samsung’s hardware prowess with designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker and will include 30 frame variations.

The Korean tech giant unveiled today that preorders have now opened, but you’ll have to check if your phone is on the compatibility list to get a pair.

The idea with this collection is that it looks like regular eyewear, not another piece of conspicuous tech strapped to your face. Gentle Monster has six different frame styles, each with a different lens treatment, whereas Warby Parker has three styles: Alden, Reid, and Wren.

Both collections come in various colors and prescription lens options. The glasses weigh around 41 grams, which is relatively lightweight for all-day wear, Samsung states.

The real attraction is more than just taking pictures without reaching for your phone. With Gemini in particular, you can identify landmarks, interpret unfamiliar objects, translate restaurant menus, and provide turn-by-turn directions through Google Maps. It can summarize meeting whiteboards and save the results to Samsung Notes.

You interact with Gemini through voice commands or by tapping the frames. The glasses can also make phone calls, read out notifications, and help with day-to-day tasks. You get a 12MP HDR camera for photos and video, two open-ear speakers, and four mics.

Qualcomm’s Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 platform is the engine behind the experience, with up to nine hours of battery life. The included charging case provides up to seven additional charges.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Warby Parker’s collection starts at $395, while Gentle Monster’s more premium frames start at $449 and go up to $489. That’s an affordable starting price compared to some rival smart glasses, but expect the final cost to be impacted by prescription options and individual frame choices.

Of course, when you start putting cameras and microphones on people’s faces, it raises some questions. Samsung says there’s an external LED that should indicate when the camera is recording, with safeguards in place to prevent it from recording if someone covers the indicator or disables it. Gemini also automatically blurs faces of bystanders in visual requests. Google says it doesn't use visuals captured for AI training or ad targeting.

There’s another catch, however: it’s not universally compatible. Supported devices are newer Samsung Galaxy phones running One UI 9 based on Android 17, Google Pixel 7 and later, and iPhone 13 Pro or later.

Preorders are now available through Google, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker ahead of its December 10 launch in the US and South Korea (Gentle Monster models only).

#414. Floods Force Gaza to Choose Between Clean Water and Pumping Out Sewage

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (835 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Floods Force Gaza to Choose Between Clean Water and Pumping Out Sewage

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Gaza floods overwhelm displacement sites, municipal teams in Al Maghazi refugee camp face a difficult trade-off: Pumping floodwaters out of shelters means taking away fuel needed to supply residents with drinkable water.
  • “The diesel we use for these pumps comes from the allocation for the wells that are supposed to pump water,” notes municipal engineer Imad Abdel Jawad, and this is at a time when their supply is already insufficient.
  • Rainstorms swept through Gaza over the weekend of November 7 and 8, overwhelming damaged sewage networks and makeshift shelters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Gaza floods overwhelm displacement sites, municipal teams in Al Maghazi refugee camp face a difficult trade-off: Pumping floodwaters out of shelters means taking away fuel needed to supply residents with drinkable water.

“The diesel we use for these pumps comes from the allocation for the wells that are supposed to pump water,” notes municipal engineer Imad Abdel Jawad, and this is at a time when their supply is already insufficient.

Rainstorms swept through Gaza over the weekend of November 7 and 8, overwhelming damaged sewage networks and makeshift shelters. In some tents in Al Maghazi, the water was well over a foot deep, Jawad indicates.

It has been revealed that for Hanan Saied, 46, the storm soaked the bedding and clothing she shares with her seven children. She lives in a shelter in Al Maghazi with mud walls, cracks, and plastic sheeting covering the roof, which WIRED Middle East visited.

It has been revealed that “The house flooded, and stones and mud fell on us,” Saied says. “The bedding was soaked, and the children’s clothes were soaked.”.

Her children used buckets to move water away while her eldest son tried to repair the shelter. Saied spent the night holding her daughter, Sara, who she states has asthma, trying to keep her warm.

Gaza’s Government Media Office has remarked at least 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians had flooded within 12 hours.

On 8 November, the Israel account on X, run by Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, posted, “Contrary to popular belief, Israel does not control the weather.” The post did not explicitly mention Gaza floods.

Industry observers note that the flooding comes after widespread destruction of Gaza’s housing. An April assessment by the European Union, United Nations, and World Bank found that more than 371,888 housing units had been damaged or destroyed and around 1.9 million people internally displaced, often repeatedly.

By 8 November, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) estimated that 1.4 million people—65 percent of Gaza’s population—were living in tents or shelters. Humanitarian partners had received appeals from more than 26,000 households whose shelters or belongings had been damaged.

Recent findings suggest that in Al Maghazi, Jawad describes five displacement sites across the camp’s western and northern areas. Parts sit on low ground where rainwater accumulates without an outlet.

In a recent development, his teams used pumps to move water outside the displacement sites. But the problems extend beneath the streets.

Israeli bombardment has damaged sewage manhole covers in Al Maghazi, Jawad notes. Other covers have been stolen or deteriorated over time. The resulting openings allow rainwater to pour into sewage networks unable to accommodate the extra volume, causing wastewater to overflow.

“The sewage networks become unable to accommodate the quantities of sewage in addition to the rainwater that leaks into the manholes because the covers are missing,” he states.

In a recent development, replacement covers are unavailable locally, while materials needed to fabricate alternatives are scarce and expensive. The municipality cannot afford all the work required. Keeping the water supply running takes priority.

“I consider spending money on maintaining wells or maintaining generators to operate water wells a higher priority than allocating some of that money to maintaining sewage manhole covers,” Jawad says.

These shortages extend across Gaza. In its November 5 report, OCHA said Israeli authorities continued to impose particularly tight restrictions on engine oil, lubricants, spare parts, and fresh generators. Systems for pumping floodwater and sewage were already failing.

Restoring more sustainable power supplies, the agency added, depended on Israeli permission to import solar panels, reconnect the electricity grid, and restart Gaza’s power plant.

The Israel Defense Forces did not respond to WIRED Middle East’s request for comment on restrictions affecting the entry of equipment and supplies needed for flood prevention and infrastructure repairs.

Jawad notes trucks and earth-moving machinery are needed to bring material to displacement sites where water collects on muddy ground, improving conditions beneath and around tents.

Sources indicate that the consequences also reach clinics. Dr Asma Saleh, a general practitioner at the Al Maghazi clinic of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), reports an increase in children presenting with respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses as the rainy season begins.

Saleh says the clinic sees around 120 children daily, including approximately 22 with influenza-like illness diagnosed from symptoms and 13 with gastroenteritis.

“The inhumane living conditions, collapse of infrastructure, the flowing streets contaminated with sewage, and the shortage of medical supplies are all factors that profoundly impact the health care system in Gaza,” she notes.

Recent findings suggest that for Saied, the immediate concern is getting Sara through the next storm. Her daughter has more frequent asthma attacks during winter, she states, and the family has neither a nebuliser nor electricity to operate one.

“My older son spent hours repairing our worn shelter using simple tools, but I don’t know what to do during upcoming storms.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app. One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years.

Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

But the “temporary” option just got a very welcome upgrade in iOS 27.

Recent findings suggest that that’s because you can now set up location sharing in Find My for a custom duration. Per Apple:.

It has been revealed that consumers [now] have more control over how they share their location with friends and family using Find My, with fresh options to share for a custom duration — either for a number of minutes, hours, or days — or even set a date and time for when sharing will stop. This makes it easy for users to share their location while attending an event, or for a long weekend getaway with friends and family.

Until iOS 27, you could only choose from a very limited set of “temporary” options for sharing: for one hour, or until end of day. The only other option was “indefinitely.”.

The main time I find myself adding new people to share my location with, I’m either traveling or they’re visiting me. On these occasions, the “one hour” and “until end of day” options never cut it.

So of course, I have to choose “indefinitely.” Then there’s the decision after the trip ends of either continuing to let location sharing happen, or ending sharing immediately (if I remember to). And the latter option has always felt a little awkward to me. I’d much rather schedule the sharing duration upfront.

And now with iOS 27 I can. When sharing location with someone, a new ‘Custom’ duration option allows choosing an end date and time, and/or manually setting a given number of days, hours, and minutes for sharing to continue.

It’s a great change, long overdue, and works perfectly for the scenarios Apple outlined.

Industry observers note that have you ever wished for custom sharing durations in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

#409. My 9 Favorite Pickleball Paddles From 3 Years of Testing (2026)

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3132 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

My 9 Favorite Pickleball Paddles From 3 Years of Testing (2026)

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The sport of pickleball—a cross between tennis and badminton, played with a hard plastic ball—is 60 years old, having been invented near Seattle in 1965.
  • Pickleball has exploded in popularity, and with that newfound popularity comes an arms race with paddle makers in a quest to make the best pickleball paddles.
  • Updated November 2026: We've added a fresh paddle from Paddletek and a couple of accessories, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The sport of pickleball—a cross between tennis and badminton, played with a hard plastic ball—is 60 years old, having been invented near Seattle in 1965. For most of that time, paddles were made of laminated wood and were mostly found in gym classes and retirement communities.

Pickleball has exploded in popularity, and with that newfound popularity comes an arms race with paddle makers in a quest to make the best pickleball paddles. Paddle technology is improving, too. This is my third year testing the latest crop of pickleball paddles, and they've made another leap forward. Among my long-standing favorite paddles like the Selkirk Vanguard Control Invikta, there are two latest ones—including the Diadem Warrior BluCore—that step back from the raw power of heat-molded plastic cores by substituting foam cores that offer a very consistent and controlled feel. Here are my most up-to-date paddle picks for every style and level of play.

Updated November 2026: We've added a fresh paddle from Paddletek and a couple of accessories, and updated links and prices.

Selkirk is a wildly popular paddle maker, but I was not a huge fan of the higher-end paddles in the lineup after testing dozens of models over a few seasons.

It has been revealed that the Selkirk Vanguard Control Invikta sold me on the brand. It’s still the best all-around paddle for most people and the one I'd recommend to anyone who doesn't demand the ability to hit huge overhead smashes—the Invikta is not thermoformed and doesn't have quite the same power as paddles that are. (Thermoformed paddles are molded with heat and injected with foam, while traditional paddles are made by stacking up layers like a sandwich.).

It has been revealed that what the Invikta offers, however, is exceptional control and consistency. This paddle is shockingly well balanced and feels great in the hand, thanks to Selkirk's upgraded octagonal grip. Every time you swing the Invikta, the hit feels like you expect it to feel, and the ball goes exactly where you expect it to go. It's especially nice to have confidence in that consistency while developing more spin (I was a practitioner of the now-banned spin toss serve and I'm still in rebuilding mode), because you don't have to worry about a goofy bounce from a dead spot caused by a botched thermoforming process. The Invikta does offer impressive spin, thanks to a T700 raw carbon face and a larger-than-average sweet spot.

According to recent reports, I was not sure what to expect from Diadem's latest BluCore paddle, which is among a handful of new paddles that have replaced the standard honeycomb polymer core with closed-cell foam—they sent me a sample of the stuff, and it looks like you could make a gas station cooler out of it. That foam is substantially more durable—it has a lifetime warranty, in fact—over the long haul and is also not at risk of delaminating in extreme temperatures if, for example, you leave the paddle in the car on a scorching summer day while you grab patio margs.

Given how far this paddle is outside the norm, and the fact that it's priced at the upper end of the range, I wanted to put real time in before recommending it. What I found was that the BluCore took some time to get used to, but it's now the paddle I play with the most. The foam core makes for a softer and more forgiving feel—it's like the suspension on an old Cadillac coupe. While I don't feel like I'm getting the most out of my serve, I especially love this paddle in defensive situations against better players. It plays consistently from edge to edge and has a nice, big sweet spot.

Whether foam ends up dominating the pickleball market remains to be seen, but people who play nearly every day will also appreciate that this paddle uses an aramid carbon fiber face that is more durable than raw carbon and that the foam absorbs more vibration.

Recent findings suggest that ★ Another foam core paddle: I was also pretty impressed with the Selkirk Labs 008, a newly introduced foam core paddle from the maker of our top pick for most people above. The 008 has a more traditional feel and a smaller but more poppy sweet spot. Because this paddle uses a T700 raw carbon fiber instead of more durable aramid carbon fiber, I fear the face will lose its effectiveness even when the core remains solid.

If you've never played pickleball, this is a good place to start, so you can get a feel for the game without sinking too much dough. For less than $30, you get two paddles and a few balls.

It has been revealed that ★ A beginner upgrade: The SLK Evo Power XL 2.0 is the paddle I bought myself from a big-box sporting goods store after a few times playing with the cheap set off Amazon. I bought this paddle based on its excellent feel and still love swinging it. Selkirk bills this paddle, which has a fiberglass face that provides limited spin, as an ideal pick for beginners and pickleball-curious tennis players.

It has been revealed that this is the fourth edition of the signature paddle made for pro pickleballer Ben Johns, the reigning number one singles player in the world. I've tested the previous two Johns' paddles along with a half-dozen others from Mayland-based Joola—including a few now-banned paddles that were the subject of a brief calamity last year.

The current Persus paddle, which is fully approved for tournament play, has a ton of pop. This paddle is thermoformed, meaning it's heat-pressed together and virtually indestructible. It’s a little heavy on the head and has less power than the previous generation, but with better control. The sweet spot is also a little larger but less sweet. Whack one right on the money, though, and the ball jolts off it.

Industry observers note that ★ Budget mashing: If you want to mash balls, but on a budget, go for the Phantom Eternal. A carbon-fiber face for $60 is a great bargain, and the Phantom Eternal is overall a very solid paddle. I didn't find it all that precise compared to competitors that are more than double the price (there are dead spots at the top of my paddle, around the eyes). However, I loved the thick, slightly sticky grip and appreciated the unique graphics. Mostly, though, I found myself swinging for the fences with this paddle—something about it makes you feel like you can smoke a return right next to your opponent's foot.

According to recent reports, full disclosure: I have never really understood the appeal of an open-throat pickleball paddle. Having a gap between the handle and paddle face that mimics a tennis racket does not provide any obvious benefit—those who have examined the claimed benefits have seemingly concluded they don't exist.

Sources indicate that however, some people like the look and feel of these paddles, so I have tested a handful and found this paddle from Onix to be the best of the bunch. It's also my pick if you want an edgeless paddle (another design quirk I don't favor). This paddle is fun to swing hard and has a very consistent face, though the two rubber inserts designed to lessen vibration aren't doing much for me, as this paddle plays very bumpy.

In a recent development, diadem's Hush is a thermoformed paddle that employs a foam-covered face to eliminate the controversial pop sound (which I love). Diadem notes it's the quietest paddle in the world; I found the noise level more akin to tennis than pickleball.

The best compliment I can give the Hush is that it handles mostly like any other paddle. This is a very welcome surprise given that its face feels like a pool noodle. The paddle only weighs 8 ounces but seems heavier. While the dense, spongy surface doesn't offer as much pop as a standard thermoformed paddle, it's got as much as the standard layer-build paddles on this list. I still haven't found any obvious dead spots, though it is understandably a little mushy. Diadem claims the foam is also helpful for spin, but in my testing I wasn't able to generate much. This paddle is not tournament-approved, but if you're looking to play at odd hours or practice against a wall at your house, it could save you a lot of drama.

Sources indicate that pickleballs are cousins to Wiffle balls. If you grew up playing backyard baseball, you probably remember that the holes in the plastic balls allowed them to spin in unpredictable ways when thrown or hit correctly. The same is true of pickleball, where a skilled player with the right paddle can cause problems for an opponent. A serve with spin is so much harder to return that the official rules of the game now ban players from swirling the ball during a drop serve.

I have not mastered topspin and backspin but the Reload has me working on the technique. The biggest problem with amateurs creating topspin is that the gritty paddles that deliver it are either technically illegal or rapidly lose effectiveness. This gets annoyingly technical very quickly, but rule 2.E.2.a of USA Pickleball's Equipment Standards manual lays out a standard and protocol for max grittiness and establishes that “a coefficient of friction test based on protocol (IAW) ASTM D1894-14 is used to measure the general friction characteristics.” Carbon fiber is the best material for getting up to the threshold but not over it, but the carbon surfaces wear down like a pencil, meaning paddles lose grittiness over time—a normal paddle loses half its grit within a month of play according to a study done by Reload's owner (who obviously has a competing product to sell). This phenomenon is well known in pickleball circles, and pro players often switch out their paddles after every game or tournament to have fresh grit.

Reload paddles offer an innovative solution by making the carbon-fiber surface replaceable. The Reload paddle itself is a very neutral and balanced middle-weight thermoformed paddle with the standard polypropylene core. The magic is in the peel-and-stick carbon fiber sheets for the hitting surface, which give you fresh grit for $50 instead of dropping another $200 and sending a months-old plastic paddle to the landfill. I found the replacement process refreshingly forgiving, as my first attempt was misaligned on one side, but I couldn't tell which side got a second stick.

Recess pickleball paddles are known for their unmatched style—these are the prettiest paddles in the game. They come in a wide variety of colorful patterns and have great grips with plenty of cushioning made from faux leather. They also come with an embroidered canvas cover.

According to recent reports, with a gritted fiberglass surface over the standard polymer honeycomb core, they do not offer the same performance as the high-end carbon-fiber pickleball paddles. Recess paddles do seem to have a smaller sweet spot than some other brands. However, when you play a shot well, this paddle is excellent. I’ll take the satisfaction of a well-played ball hit with a stylish Recess paddle over almost anything on this list.

Because I'm always testing fresh paddles, I usually roll up to the courts with about $2,000 worth of high-end paddles in my Babolat bag. My 10-year-old daughter can pick any paddle she wants, and the one she likes best is this $43 paddle from Pickle Genius. At 13 millimeters, it's a little thinner than most paddles here, which means she can swing faster and harder. It has a very neutral feel, mid-grade pop, and simple design.

Here are some other paddles we've really liked in testing, including some older models still on sale still worth considering.

In a recent development, paddletek Honeyfoam ESQ 16 mm for $100: The day I first began testing this paddle, it stopped my singles partner dead in her tracks. “What is that?” “Paddletek Honeyfoam.” “Don’t they all have honeycomb?” “No, honey-FOAM.” Three foam types do make for a larger sweet spot as promised, and the softer surface makes for a slower ball and increased control. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar liked the classic “pop” sound, and so do I, so it’s a little sad to hear it muffled here, but I’ll take the softer thwack if it means I can catch the ball a little off-center and still put it where I want it. —Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that joola's Tyson McGuffin Magnus 3 for $248: This previous pick is still available used. Joola not only has the top-ranked player in the world but also number six, Tyson McGuffin. What I love about the McGuffin signature paddle is the sound. You may know that the sound of a pickleball game is quite controversial. I happen to like the sound (I do not live next to a pickleball court), and I like the sound of this paddle best of all. The hot-pink McGuffin paddle is one of the hottest on the market right now and frequently out of stock. It's a banger, using “Propulsion Core technology” that offers serious power, and I find myself too often hitting long with it. However, that sound. Pawwwwp. It's so satisfying. Pawwwwp. It sounds like a well-hit baseball by your favorite team to walk off in the bottom of the ninth.

Industry observers note that bagsmart Advantage 15L Paddle Tote for $21: I’ve been carrying this sturdy bag for almost a full season now, and it somehow looks just as pristine as the day I got it. Though the styling is quite loud (people sometimes think it’s a 4th of July or America-themed bag), it’s comfortable to carry with two sets of handles: short and over-the-shoulder. It’s also got a thick, rubbery bottom so you can put it right on the ground even when the court is wet. There’s also a luggage pass-through and plenty of room for a laptop, change of clothes, and multiple paddles. (Plus a water bottle holder.) —Kat Merck.

Sqairz XRZ2 Pickleball Shoes for $159: Though best known for golf shoes, Sqairz as a brand is known for its square toe box, which allows for toes to naturally splay out during play. My favorite part is that the laces have rubbery little nubs on them to keep them from coming untied. The fit seems small at first, but they stretch out fast—maybe even too much, as I have narrow feet and I’m starting to feel like there’s too much movement in them. I'd consider going a half-size down. That noted, I do appreciate the sole's stability, even if they're a bit heavy. —Kat Merck.

I’m not an expert player (I'm somewhere between a 4.0 and a 4.5 on the USAP's Player Skill Rating), but I’ve now tested more than 100 paddles on indoor and outdoor courts over the past three years. At one point I played in a weekly pickleball league, though I don't anymore. I also test the paddles against a Slinger pickleball machine which is very helpful, as the machine consistently fires balls with a lot of spin and power. After playing with piles of paddles—and having players of various skill levels try them and share their thoughts—I feel confident that this guide has a paddle recommendation for you, whether you're a beginner or a pro pickleball player.

Pickleball paddles are restricted by a size formula similar to the one airlines use: The paddle can’t be longer than 17 inches and the combined length and width of the paddle cannot exceed 24 inches. A standard paddle is 16 inches long and 8 inches wide, but some elongated paddles use the full 17 inches and tend to have more power than wider options. There is no restriction on the thickness of the paddle; thin paddles can be about one-third of an inch thick, while thick paddles can be up to three-quarters of an inch thick.

It has been revealed that you'll see me using this term a few times in this guide. “Pop” is the pickleball parlance for how aggressively the ball bounces off the paddle face—you can think of it as an analogue to how "bouncy" a basketball is.

The latest buzzword in pickleball circles is “dwell time,” which means how long the ball stays in contact with the face of the paddle before bouncing back off. Because your body is providing torque when you swing, the longer the balls sits—time measured in nanoseconds—on the face of the paddle the more spin will be created and the harder your shot will be to return. It gets very nerdy very quickly. I would love to speak about the dwell time of the paddles I've tested, but my personal sense of the number of nanoseconds the ball is in contact with the paddle is not appropriately fine-tuned.

How Much Do Pickleball Paddles Weigh?

There is no rule about a pickleball paddle's weight, but almost every paddle hovers around 8 ounces. I went out of my way to test the biggest range of paddles I could find and ended up testing paddles that were within about an ounce of each other. Light paddles tend to be about 7.5 ounces, whereas heavyweight paddles are about 8.5 ounces. More important is the distribution of that weight—paddles that offer more power tend to be top-heavy. I prefer paddles with a balanced feel.

Are All Pickleball Paddles the Same Shape?

In a recent development, pickleball paddles tend to look fairly similar shapewise. In my testing, I tried several outliers, including a Joola paddle with a rounded shape more like a tennis racket, and several Selkirk paddles with a cutout between the paddle face and handle designed to minimize air resistance. I think the standard shape is still best.

What Are Pickleball Paddles Made Of?

In a recent development, old-fashioned wooden paddles still exist, but inexpensive fiberglass paddles are how I started playing. You can nab a beginner set for $30 (see “Best for Beginners”), and it could be six months before you feel the need to upgrade. That mentioned, the paddles recommended here tend to have a carbon-fiber face, which is stiff and light, offering lots of pop. I also tested some graphite paddles, which are cheaper, heavier, and softer than carbon fiber. If your budget doesn’t allow you to start with carbon fiber, I’d recommend starting with cheap fiberglass and then jumping to carbon fiber. Note that when I mention materials, I mean what's used for the face of the paddle—nearly all paddles have a similar honeycomb-shaped polymer core. Pricier paddles tend to cut that core in a way that creates even gaps on the edge and use heat-pressing to seal the face to the core.

If you're new to exploring kinks and fetishes online, it can be a weird and intimidating experience. But it's also exciting, which is why it's worth exploring deeper.

What you need is the right platform to get started. There are great sites and apps out there that offer sexy fun with like-minded folk. It doesn't matter if you have specialist kinks for feet, spanking, or BDSM — or even a relatively vanilla taste for threesomes — you can find your tribe somewhere online.

Recent findings suggest that experienced fet-lovers will already know that regular dating apps just don't cut it. So, the question is, how do you connect with similarly-minded kinksters? The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections Tinder — top pick for fast hookups Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups Pure — best for anonymous hookups OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

According to recent reports, we strongly recommend two platforms for exploring your favorite kinks and more. Those platforms are AdultFriendFinder and FetLife, both of which are stacked with NSFW content. Seriously, do not log on to these in public. And who knows? You might even discover a few kinks you never even knew you had.

Maybe you just don't know what you're into yet. But if you want to find a safe, non-judgmental space to explore your options and go on a journey of sexual self-discovery, these are the places to do it.

Before we get deep into the pros and cons of AFF and FetLife, let us share some general information with you. AdultFriendFinder and FetLife both skew male, which is fairly standard across the online dating spectrum. The average user on FetLife is aged 25, while AdultFriendFinder customers tend to be in their 30s. Even so, both sites offer a diverse range of genders and ages — not to mention a colorful range of sexual orientations and kink communities. In other words, there really is something for everyone.

But while both sites are designed to accommodate sex-positive communities and make connections between kinksters, they have their own way of doing things. You may find that one site suits you better than the other, though we recommend trying both on for size to see which one fits.

Keep reading for a rundown of the major differences between AFF and FetLife and decide which one to try first.

Recent findings suggest that fetLife is very popular, but be aware that it can take time to build a following and earn trust on the site. While it's possible to message strangers, the site culture discourages it. Don't be surprised if unsolicited messages are ignored completely. AdultFriendFinder, on the other hand, is a DM-sliding free-for-all. In fact, the concept of connecting with strangers is kind of the point. In that respect, AFF operates like a regular dating site (it's one of the OGs in that field, dating back to 1996), whereas FetLife is more of a social media website for building local kink communities.

AdultFriendFinder also hosts live webcam demonstrates and community discussion forums, offering owners multiple ways to connect rapidly. There's more to it than just one-on-one.

This one might be controversial, since the AFF site is notoriously dated, but FetLife's interface is downright confusing, a mix between Facebook and Instagram, with much more limited search functionality. While both sites will allow you to search by specific kinks (and both sites offer exhaustive lists of kink options), the search functionality and filter options on AdultFriendFinder are more comprehensive and more user-friendly.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't an accident, by the way. FetLife deliberately disables search by age, gender, and sexual orientation because, in their words, they are "a social network and not a dating site.".

Sources indicate that remember that AFF looks and feels dated because it's been around for three decades and has kept things very old school indeed. AFF doesn't even have an app — it's website only. Be warned that the interface is chock-full of nudity and NSFW content.

FetLife allows people to host videos, but it doesn't have a dedicated, live webcam service. Some FetLife users will offer that, but they do this on third-party sites, and usually behind a paywall. AFF, on the other hand, makes live streaming a significant part of its community experience and allows you to search through webcam shows by the streamer's location or the show's interest/topic, which often revolves around a specific kink.

In other words, if you're content to watch, AFF delivers some excellent, kink-centric live action, and much of it is accessible without upgrading to a paid subscription.

According to recent reports, the most noticeable difference between FetLife and AFF is how much more freedom is afforded to non-paying accounts. On AdultFriendFinder, profiles are locked behind a paywall, so only paying members can scroll through photos, view bios, and see a comprehensive list of kinks. FetLife, on the other hand, operates more like Instagram for kinksters. It delivers large photos, comprehensive bios, and even a web of connections comparable to what you might see on Facebook, from friends and romantic partners to subs, doms, and mentors, if applicable.

Even more important, free FetLife users can contact each other in one-on-one messages without having to give up their credit card information, which definitely makes it easier to establish a personal connection.

One major limitation of free accounts is that users can't watch videos. Because raunchy videos are a mainstay on many profiles, this is definitely a hindrance, though it's not a deal-breaker.

Perhaps the biggest benefit of FetLife over AdultFriendFinder is that the former is much more focused on real-life connections, whereas AdultFriendFinder seems content to let people play in the virtual world.

The Events tab at the top of the FetLife banner allows you to see, at a glance, all of the nearby, kink-friendly events, from informal meet-and-greets to full-on costume and masquerade balls. Best of all, you can filter by sub-type (Party, Educational, Social, Conference/Festival, Sex Party) or just look for events that your FetLife friends are attending.

Sources indicate that these in-person events are integral to the FetLife experience, even when the events aren't officially affiliated with the site itself. In fact, it's pretty common to see people indicate, in their profiles, that they won't message or "friend" anyone they haven't already met at an IRL event.

Because of its community emphasis and dedication to exploring sexuality in a safe, consensual, and informed way, FetLife offers owners not only the means to connect with others but also to better connect with themselves. There's the community-sourced Kinktionary, for example, a Wiki-like resource covering topical aspects of human sexuality from the ins and outs of gay culture to a comprehensive list of sex toys and their uses, as well as dedicated groups to not only explore kinks but also introduce people to the BDSM lifestyle (we recommend you check out the Novices & Newbies section if you're a first-time visitor).

AdultFriendFinder isn't totally without these resources, but they're not as user-friendly or as accessible to total newcomers to the world of kink.

According to recent reports, both AFF and FetLife are among the very best online destinations for kink-based fun. They have their pros, cons, and differences, but you're unlikely to go wrong with either. They each have large user bases and comprehensive selections of kink-focused spaces. That helps create a non-judgmental atmosphere, allowing you to let go of any sense of inhibition. Just let loose and enjoy yourself doing it.

It has been revealed that that said, if you're looking for the fastest possible connection and you're happy to keep things strictly online for now, AdultFriendFinder is the place to start. If, on the other hand, you want to integrate into your local kink community and get on the guest lists of underground fetish clubs or VIP sex parties, FetLife can make that happen.

#407. Tech Report: The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2474 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 would be my perfect Steam tablet if it didn’t cost $900

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2474 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory.
  • Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM.
  • But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For every Android-powered slate I’ve used, only Nvidia’s Shield Tablet really stands out in my memory. Part of the firm’s occasional (and all-but-dead) dip into hardware products, the Shield Tablet — and its revitalized K1 follow-up, which I also owned through a recall program on the original — carried me through the back half of college, frequently keeping my Chromebook in my backpack in lieu of a mini Bluetooth keyboard or the Shield Tablet’s built-in stylus. Its front-firing speakers made it great for movie-watching, and while I’m not much of a mobile gamer, I did find it to be a great device for emulation, especially when paired with an external controller.

Even if Nvidia hadn’t abandoned the hardware game at the end of the last decade, it’s found new and much more destructive ways to make piles of cash at the expense of your easy access to RAM. And considering the market for Android tablets in general, it’s not all too surprising to see very few companies trying to make headway into offering a miniature, gaming-focused tablet that can easily be thrown in a backpack. Lenovo, however, has managed to fill its spot quite well. 9to5Google’s own Ben Schoon found himself smitten with the Gen 3 model nearly two years ago, and now, its Gen 5 successor has found its way into my nostalgic hands.

But expectations around mobile experiences have come a long way since 2016. Whether the Legion Tab Gen 5 can win over your heart really depends on your patience with some old-school Android jank — and whether your wallet can withstand an exceptionally-high asking price. Still, with recent advancements in PC emulation, it’s hard to say Lenovo isn’t onto something.

Considering the decade between their respective releases, I’m actually quite surprised just how much this tablet reminds me of the original Shield Tablet. Its 8.8-inch 16:10 LCD panel combined with a boxy matte-black design and a near-identical weight meant that I immediately felt at home holding this thing in my hands. You lose out on a couple of clutch features — most notably the built-in stylus — but largely speaking, this feels like the correct size and shape for a miniature gaming tablet.

Sources indicate that still, it’s not all perfect. Take, for example, the completely unnecessary camera bump that prevents this slate from properly laying flat on a desk. No one is buying this thing to use the camera, and judging by my very limited experience trying it out, I’m fairly confident whatever potato sensor is shoved in here would fit fine flush with the chassis. I’m pretty fed up with OEMs leaning on camera bumps to make any device look or feel more premium than it actually is, and that goes double quadruple for tablets like this.

Just like its predecessor, this thing still picks up smudges and fingerprints at an unreasonable level, its matte-black finish unable to hide anything. 360 grams is also a little heavier than I’d expect for a slate of this size, though to be fair, it’s much more noticeable in portrait than landscape. Holding the tablet with two hands to watch a movie or make my way through another round of Balatro made its top-heaviness much less noticeable.

This display is sharp and fast — with one minor caveat — and reasonably bright in all circumstances except direct sunlight thanks to its 600 nits of brightness (and 800 in HBM). Really, it’s the LCD of it all that gets me here; this thing is nearly $1,000, and the lack of OLED alone makes it difficult to recommend at this price. It’s not an outright bad panel, but I found its contrast levels to be pretty lacking, with most blacks only ever showing up as dark grays on-screen.

It has been revealed that oh, and that caveat: On two different occasions, I caught the tablet stuck in 60Hz mode, regardless of what refresh rate option I selected in settings. Switching back and forth between modes a few times eventually unstuck it, but it’s definitely a bug worth being aware of.

I think I’d feel a lot better about recommending this to someone looking for a content consumption device if this screen looked a little more premium. Your mileage may vary though — if you can get your hands on a demo unit before buying one, if only to see the display, I’d recommend it. For everyone else, this price tag might have you waiting for the OLED panel rumored to be arriving on next year’s successor.

At $900 — or potentially more, considering this tablet actually rolled out at $850 — the Legion Tablet’s hardware leaves something to be desired. Biometrics are the most obvious weak spot; camera-based face unlock is the only biometric option provided here, without a fingerprint scanner in sight. I wouldn’t blame some if they saw this as a dealbreaker, because even if you’re willing to put up with the security concerns that a basic front-facing camera brings to the table, I can promise you you’ll be typing the code in all the time. Whether you’re trying to unlock in a darker environment or it’s just been four hours since you last unlocked the slate, make sure you have your pin memorized.

According to recent reports, if you’re primarily buying this as a content consumption machine, I think you’ll mostly have a great time. Lenovo built stereo sound into this slate, but did so in one of the smartest ways I’ve ever seen, ensuring all speakers are located to the right side along the bottom and top of the device. This might sound a little unbalanced in portrait mode, but in landscape, it guarantees you’re never actually covering up the speakers while holding the slate in your hands, something practically every other equivalent tablet is guilty of. No headphone jack here, unfortunately, something I would’ve liked to have seen on a gaming-focused device.

Sources indicate that I find battery life genuinely difficult to judge on tablets, especially if you don’t pick it up every single hour of every single day, but I’ve been impressed overall with the Legion Tab’s longevity. Some weekend YouTube binge watching sessions at relatively high brightness settings left me with plenty of juice in the tank, and its standby time between sessions has been excellent. Obviously, if you’re really pushing your graphical limits on this thing — or if you’re emulating non-native software through something like DroidDeck — you’re going to see a bit of a dip, but combined with fast charging and two USB-C ports for both portrait and landscape access, battery life gets a big thumbs-up from me.

Lenovo’s packed a couple of accessories in the box with this thing, but I wouldn’t get too excited. While it’s nice to see a 68W charger included for those aforementioned fast top-offs, the included folio case is just awful. Not only does the triangle-shaped flap barely stick together to form a proper stand, but one of the corners of my case was loose enough to frequently flex back and forth. Holding the tablet while wrapped in its case just felt bad, in the way that so many bundled cases often feel, and a quick look at Amazon demonstrates that basically no recognizable brand — or unrecognizable, for that matter — has stepped up to offer something better.

The Legion Tablet also includes a screen protector in the box, if that’s how you roll.

Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 in here can handle effectively anything you dare to throw at it. While my mobile games might be limited to more casual, indie fare like Balatro — and, by the by, if you’re still enjoying Balatro a couple of years later, the size and shape of this device makes it perfect — graphically-intense games played fine. Asphalt Legends or the HoYoverse games might not be my cup of tea, but they perform excellently on this device, and compared to the 12-inch tablets companies like Samsung and Amazon have become obsessed with, the display size here actually feels perfect.

Sources indicate that we definitely have to talk about emulation, though, because it’s increasingly becoming the main focus of mobile gamers everywhere, and this feels like a tablet perfectly designed for something like DroidDeck. Getting Steam emulation — complete with the Deck’s usual Big Picture mode UI — available as an application on the Legion Tab Gen 5 takes all of two minutes and a handful of taps on your display, and I have to say, I’m pretty shocked at just how impressive the overall experience is right now.

Recent findings suggest that droidDeck gave me the option to bring my mini gaming tablet experience full-circle. While my Steam library has no shortage of games I think could run without stressing this slate, I wanted to push the envelope a little bit. Persona 3 Reload felt like as good a candidate as any: a modern title that doesn’t necessarily require quick response times and fits virtual controls quite nicely. Plus, most of my gaming time on Nvidia’s tablet a decade ago was spent working through Persona 3 Portable; like poetry, it rhymes. I installed the game, ran it on the Legion Tab, and to my surprise and delight, it was absolutely in a playable state.

According to recent reports, now, there are some caveats here. I did drop the game’s graphics preset to low, and even still, there were some occasional hiccups while running around an early dungeon. The game’s initial intros and disclaimers actually gave the impression the title wouldn’t run at all, but I was able to sneak up on a shadow, use a slash attack to begin the battle — basically the only thing in P3R that remotely requires accurate timing — and issue commands to my player character and party mates.

In a recent development, obviously, your experience emulating Steam titles on the Legion Tab will vary on what you want to play, and with such wide variables between experiences, I probably wouldn’t push most gamers to run out and pick one up right away. It might be early days for DroidDeck, but considering how we’ve already seen it progress, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some buyers picking this up as a Valve-esque take on a gaming tablet.

It has been revealed that with all of that power under the hood, though, it’s Lenovo’s take on Android that leaves a lot to be desired. It’s not just that this feels like a rough-and-ready take on AOSP, an unrefined package that would feel more in line with devices from a decade ago, though, yes, that’s half the struggle here. But at its worst, the Legion Tab Gen 5 simply feels unoptimized in daily use.

According to recent reports, scrolling through web pages or various apps often felt sluggish and heavy, like the UI elements on screen never actually match the movement of my finger, and it’s unclear how much of that was due to the refresh rate bug I described above. Auto-rotate was both super finnicky and super sluggish, alternating back and forth between one state or the other, and the auto-rotate button that pops up when it’s disabled would frequently fail to appear. Occasionally, I’d run into app problems, such as choppy playback on a 1440p YouTube video that got so bad — regardless of what resolution I selected — that I had to fully force close the app in settings to fix it. Even getting the slate to reliably wake up (or not wake up) when picking it up was annoying, as it’s simultaneously sensitive enough to frequently turn on when I don’t want it to, or to stay asleep when I’m trying to unlock it. Inevitably, I turned that setting off.

Sources indicate that you might think that shelling out $900 for an Android tablet would buy you an out from pre-installed bloatware; you’d be wrong. During setup, the Legion Tab attempts to install a whole host of apps and games, including Perplexity, TikTok, Temu, several match-three games that I’ve truly never heard of, and no less than two mahjong and solitaire titles each. In fact, there might actually be three solitaire titles depending on what “Jigsawcard Solitaire Puzzle” is, but I unchecked all of these apps during setup and didn’t deem the title worthy of bothering to check.

While Lenovo has been trying to improve its software update policies on some recent devices, this slate isn’t among that group. To my knowledge, there is no official update schedule for this device, but based on past performance, I’d expect somewhere around 2 OS upgrades and 4 years of security patches, give or take.

I would’ve loved nothing more than to recommend this year’s Legion Tab to small tablet fans and gamers everywhere, but when this thing is $200 more than Apple’s latest iPad Mini — which in and of itself is absolutely overpriced — and $100 more than the base OLED Steam Deck post-price hike, I just have a hard time telling anyone to buy it. Really, its Steam performance was one of the few areas that made me feel truly excited by this thing, but it’s simply too unpredictable an experience at this point (and price) for me to recommend.

Even setting aside the price, there’s simply too much here that feels unfinished or rough around the edges for my liking. A handful of bug fixes and a couple of additional optimization passes could fix a lot of my more minor quibbles, but despite what I just remarked, you can only ignore the $900 price tag for so long before it bites you in the ass.

In a recent development, we have seen a post-iPad Mini discount bringing this slate to an Apple-matching $700 ahead of the holidays, but even that price is $150 more than its predecessor was at launch without a whole lot to show for it. If you’re looking for a gamer-friendly tiny tablet, I do think Legion is a brand worth keeping your eye on, especially as DroidDeck and other Steam emulation apps continue to evolve. But at this point — and for this price — your best bet is waiting for whatever model follows this one. It might still be stupid expensive, but at least you’ll be getting OLED.

A decade ago, Nvidia’s Shield Tablet felt like a no-brainer addition to my everyday carry. But in this economy, gamers and tablet fans alike are simply better off dropping $900 elsewhere.

  • Over a hundred thousand frustrated people were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revision (Nov 13, 6:57 am ET): Microsoft indicates recovery efforts are now in phases, with some affected infrastructure already back online and traffic slowly returning to normal. Initially, the company blamed high infrastructure loads across many regions, but the investigation eventually revealed a more specific problem with automated server health checks. The tech giant has revealed that automated server health checks misfired, kicking healthy infrastructure offline and triggering cascading connection failures across Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot. There are automated health checks that can detect failing hardware and take it out of rotation before your inbox breaks. Instead, a particular server component that does those checks started failing its own tests. Multiple regions lost their healthy servers, and the rest of the infrastructure buckled under heavier-than-usual loads, preventing users around the world from loading their mailboxes or sending messages. Now, Microsoft’s recovery playbook relies on working around its referee. Engineers made a targeted change to work around the faulty health-check component on some servers to see if they would stay online, while rolling out safeguards to stop other machines from dropping out. Automated recovery systems have been activated to minimize the disruption, and teams are also working in parallel to rebuild the affected servers with previous configurations.

Over a hundred thousand frustrated people were left with broken inboxes and unable to get work done as Microsoft Outlook went down on Thursday, November 12.

Outlook owners in the Americas began reporting they could not access their Exchange Online mailboxes, and the complaints were rolling in fast, with Downdetector reporting more than 125,000 complaints as of this writing.

According to recent reports, if you attempted to refresh your inbox only to be greeted by infinite loading screens, you were not the only one. People are reporting being completely locked out of their accounts across desktop apps, web browsers, and mobile clients. Microsoft’s official 365 Status account confirmed the hiccup on X, blaming Exchange Online, the cloud backbone that powers your Outlook email, calendar, and contacts.

We're investigating reports of consumers experiencing complications accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.November 12, 2026.

The firm initially mentioned the connection failures were limited to the Americas, but the company later confirmed that the connectivity bug could be hitting users in just about any region.

The problem is due to the way Outlook clients authenticate and connect to Exchange Online mailboxes using different connection methods.

Microsoft engineers are currently scrambling to resolve problems on the server end and mitigate the impact, but the manufacturer has not yet provided a concrete timeline for a full fix.

Sources indicate that apps in Microsoft 365 that rely on the same service connectivity may also be slow or throw error codes until the dust settles, though Exchange Online takes the biggest hit. For now, the best course of action is to keep an eye on the official Microsoft 365 status feed, enjoy a rare, guilt-free excuse to ignore your boss’s emails, and wait for the servers to wake back up.

Latest Update: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a fresh wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.
  • According to a latest report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”.
  • AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a fresh wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a latest report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”.

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite claims that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate owners and email, and address network security problems.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

It has been revealed that enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs.

According to recent reports, it’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security challenges.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.
