#402. No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2349 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the fresh air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote.
  • New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway.
  • None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the fresh air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration rapidly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.”.

New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms.

None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.

According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?

It has been revealed that depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” claims a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.”.

Industry observers note that aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that fresh infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other.

Industry observers note that in 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed.

Joby’s aircraft flying past Lower Manhattan, Newly introduced York, in April.

Industry observers note that with a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, substantial players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia. The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia. Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come.

In a recent development, around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year.

Recent findings suggest that for more than a decade, various eVTOL builders have been promising that production models were just around the corner. But deadlines kept getting pushed back. As it turned out, engineering a flying autonomous robot was just part of the overall problem. You also needed to design an airspace that they could operate in, train humans to pilot or supervise them, develop an economic framework within which they could earn money, and so on. “It's a very notable, safe, careful dance,” notes Greg Bowles, Chief Policy Officer at Joby Aviation.

Silicon Valley’s speed has long been in conflict with air travel norms. “Aviation regulation has been conservative and prioritizes reliability, because the consequences of failure are severe,” indicates Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general in the Department of Transportation. “Certification standards and airworthiness require proof and demonstrated safety, and that usually means incremental rather than radical change.” The FAA was in no rush to let unproven robots go careening around the national airspace.

Recent findings suggest that AI faced another kind of resistance in Europe. In 2017, aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Dassault asked the EASA, the European Union’s version of the FAA, to consider allowing airliners to operate with a single pilot in the cockpit. Traditionally, airliners require multiple pilots to divide the considerable workload of flying a plane and to ensure that if one pilot becomes incapacitated, the other can carry on. In Airbus’ vision, automated systems would shoulder the copilot’s workload and even take over entirely if needed.

It has been revealed that that idea horrified pilots. The European Cockpit Association, a union of airline pilots, lodged a strong protest. Such a move “would remove an independent safety professional from the flight deck and give operators greater influence over the safety judgments that a pilot would otherwise make,” the union explained to me in an email. Last year, EASA shelved the proposal.

In a recent development, nevertheless, AI pressed onward. In 2023, the FAA began issuing waivers to allow delivery-drone flights beyond the visual range of operators; by the end of this year it could make the rule change permanent. Some of the biggest players are already pushing ahead aggressively. This past August, Amazon confirmed that it planned to expand its drone delivery service to 500 locations across the country by the end of the year. Walmart is planning drone delivery from 270 store locations by the end of 2027.

Industry observers note that the ultimate goal is far larger. Industry insiders say that in a maximal vision of the technology’s build-out, hundreds of thousands of drones will be servicing most or all of the US population. “In five to 10 years, it’s going to be completely ubiquitous,” Anthony Vittone, chief operating officer of the drone technology company DroneUp, told me in a story for Sherwood News last year. “People are going to be, like, ‘I don’t know how I lived without it.’”.

Joby and other eVTOL companies haven’t progressed quite as fast, but they, too, are moving ahead. In April, Joby flew the first-ever point-to-point eVTOL flight within Upcoming York City, from John F. Kennedy Airport to three heliports in Manhattan. The company has carried out similar flights in California and Texas, all under the auspices of the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), a federal initiative rolled out by the Trump administration this past March to demonstrate the capabilities of modern drones and eVTOLs.

These demo flights, Bowles notes, are just the “front edge” of the Joby S4’s operational rollout. Next will come demonstration flights with nonpaying passengers, demonstration flights with paying passengers, and finally flights that will take passengers from A to B. “All of that is permitted under eIPP, with increasing levels of oversight,” he says.

It has been revealed that to start, these flights will have human pilots, but it’s very expensive to pay one human to fly around a handful of paying passengers. Ultimately, for the eVTOL concept to be viable economically, all such aircraft will have to fly themselves. And if self-driving is a tough challenge for cars, it’s all the more so for aircraft, where an unexpected control system failure isn’t just dangerous but likely deadly.

According to recent reports, given the scale of the challenge, the entry point of AI into human passenger flight won’t be as flashy as piloting eVTOLs; it’ll occupy a more modest, behind-the-scenes role. Already, data companies like Palantir and aviation industry stalwarts like Jeppesen and Thales are selling AI-enabled software that lets regulators, airlines, and flight dispatchers sift through masses of data to identify risks and plan aircraft and crew scheduling.

In a recent development, in September, the FAA unveiled that it deployed software built by the Boston-based data company Air Space Intelligence. The upcoming AI-powered tool is called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” or SMART, and it’s aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” The program isn’t intended to replace controllers, the government indicates, but to make doing their jobs easier by using predictive AI to head off scheduling snags. “Combining SMART with our ongoing hardware upgrades gives us the tools to cut flight delays, optimize traffic, and keep airspace capacity across the country open—all while maintaining our gold standard of safety,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford noted in a press release.

Joby Aviation’s S4 electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft.

The system is supposed to help controllers make decisions, not make those decisions for them. But if the program feeds nonsensical information into the system, will human operators be able to catch the mistake? “This is the Trump/DOGE/Musk effect,” says the recently retired FAA employee, who asked to remain anonymous. “They’re pushing through all this upcoming technology without any understanding of the complexity of the national airspace system.”.

Recent findings suggest that some lawmakers are also concerned about SMART. On October 13, almost two dozen Democratic lawmakers reportedly sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking it to review the program, citing fears that it might “hallucinate safety-critical information.”.

In a recent development, then there’s the question of whether SMART could worsen the chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. The FAA hopes that the technology lessens the shortage by requiring fewer workers; other industries, though, have yet to see AI-generated efficiencies actually materialize. Even if the software doesn’t directly replace humans, the efficiency could be used to justify a workforce reduction. In May, the FAA reduced its staffing target for active air traffic controllers from the 2024 goal of 14,633 down to 12,563, citing “modern staffing models and scheduling tools.”.

In a recent development, some are more optimistic than others. “I think the SMART program is an crucial improvement,” Schiavo says. “No one wants the current aviation environment with midairs, runway incursions, myriad near misses, delays, groundings, loss of separation, and long taxi or clearance wait times.”.

Sources indicate that michael McCormick, a professor of air traffic management at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, also sees advantages to a predictive tool. “When you have the computing capability to look at the entire trajectory of the aircraft, you can see where the conflicts are going to be,” he says. “And the general axiom in air traffic control is that the sooner you know about a potential conflict, the less effort is required to resolve it.”.

According to recent reports, that sounds great, but building machines that do a good job most of the time is one thing; machines that can function at the level of reliability required by aviation is another. At present, researchers are focusing on so-called deterministic neural networks—models trained offline whose weights are frozen before being deployed in the real world. These can’t hallucinate, but they may harbor other risky failure modes. In a 2021 paper, Darren Cofer, a researcher at Collins Aerospace, pointed out that when such systems find themselves in situations they haven’t encountered before in training, they can generate “unexpected (and potentially dangerous) outputs.”.

The stakes will be even higher when AI software starts making real-time air traffic control decisions, which will start in airspace devoted to autonomous aircraft. According to McCormick, that’ll most likely be select corridors near drone hubs and eVTOL vertiports. With swarms of robot aircraft zipping back and forth, things will be too hairy for human pilots and controllers. “The objective is not to use traditional air traffic control,” he says, “because it would overwhelm the national airspace system if it tried to handle that volume and complexity of airframes moving around.”.

With two systems working side by side—one with human decisionmakers, the other with AI—we’ll have a real-time basis to compare the performance of both approaches. Any computer-based system can potentially be hacked; any AI system creative enough to ideate novel solutions could also hallucinate crucial details. Without a human in the loop, seemingly obvious mistakes might go unnoticed until it’s too late.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Ring confirmed the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.
  • Also: Amazon’s upcoming Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home.
  • Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Ring confirmed the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s upcoming Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home.

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both newly introduced robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

Sources indicate that the Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

It has been revealed that that makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s upcoming Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works.

There’s one other very vital caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other glitch).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

According to recent reports, the Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

Industry observers note that the other product Ring unveiled is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today.

According to recent reports, if another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

According to recent reports, even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.

Good morning. Today I’m finding open source alternatives to all of my apps, poring through Pitchfork’s list of the 100 best indie rock albums to find ones I haven’t listened to, and preparing my body for November 19th by pre-loading GTA VI (and replaying GTA IV in the meantime).

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

In a recent development, on Monday, I unboxed the iPhone Duo I pre-ordered back in October and experienced a disarming sense of déjà vu. It’s beautiful hardware married to a messy, often painful software onboarding experience atypical of Apple’s usual polish. It reminds me of the Galaxy Fold’s early years.

Recent findings suggest that I was most looking forward to the combination of a foldable form factor and Apple’s superior app ecosystem, but even the apps that have been updated to support the fresh aspect ratio, on both the front and back, feel ungainly and buggy. In moving UI elements from the bottom to the right, even with the display open, the Duo forces a rebuilding of essential muscle memory that’s prevailed across mobile platforms, including Android foldables, for 20 years.

In a recent development, the front display, in particular, is a massive test of one’s patience: apps, even ones ostensibly optimized for its stout dimensions, often feel unusable, with UI elements that would be prominent on the iPhone 18 Pro hidden behind overflow menus on the Duo. It’s exasperating and, frankly, boggling.

But what’s interesting is the enthusiasm with which developers are approaching the newly introduced form factor. Reddit threads reveal dozens of Duo-optimized app recommendations that feel novel and, if not polished, then propulsive. There’s a fascinating delta between waiting for my bank, or Starbucks, or Kobo, to get its act together to support the Duo and seeking out net-new opportunities and experiences.

I spent most of the summer using the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and I didn’t expect going back to it to feel so stately and predictable: the showcase of a platform with fewer highs but none of the Duo’s current lows.

I’m not sure if I’m going to keep the Duo and wait out its colicky infancy. But I do know that until now I hadn’t given Samsung enough credit for the amount of work it did to make foldable software feel ordinary, and that’s the highest compliment I can pay.

It competes directly with XTEINK’s excellent X4 Pro, which features a rudimentary touchscreen and backlight for around $100, though its magnets are built in.

Both products are wonderful examples of hardware companies adapting to the growing size and complexity of smartphones and seeing an opening for single-purpose products that do one thing really well. Plus, it’s fun to stick a thing to the back of your phone and… read it.

Articles live in books, links sit on a notice board, and his about page is a letter in a lighthouse. The Context Island is an incredibly thoughtful and unique approach to “web” design, and it’s another example of how AI can really help bring crazy ideas to fruition.

  • It has been revealed that also: Ready for a Siri AI agent?
  • In a recent development, with App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the many benefits of the newly introduced Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

It has been revealed that also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade.

In a recent development, with App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the fresh developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now.

Recent findings suggest that “Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple remarked in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”.

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the latest and full Siri AI integration.

Industry observers note that I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”.

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”.

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”.

In a recent development, right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV demonstrates, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps.

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

Sources indicate that I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped.

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are presently available to borrow.”.

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in Upcoming York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”.

Recent findings suggest that as my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry.

Asking Siri to tackle those tasks would certainly be a time saver. I could ask it to “find the closest Italian restaurants using Yelp and show me ones within a one-mile radius that have earned four stars or higher.”.

With App Intents, Siri AI can already handle advanced, complex, multi-step tasks for built-in apps. With all developers now able to take advantage of this same support, I’m expecting a lot of apps to jump on board. Let’s hope my favorites end up on the list.

It has been revealed that opera today announced that its Data Saver feature is now available on iOS, in a press release that also revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in the browser’s monthly active consumers. Here are the details.

In a press release published today, Opera celebrated a 20% year-over-year increase in monthly active users on iOS last month, “building on its established presence in Asia and Africa while expanding its reach in the US and Europe.”.

In the US alone, growth was even stronger, with monthly active users increasing 46% year over year.

In both cases, that outpaced the 16% year-over-year growth Opera reported on PC just a few days ago, when the company also announced it had surpassed 100 million monthly active owners for the first time.

Behind this growth across both desktop and mobile is a broader shift in consumer expectations – users are increasingly reconsidering the default as their understanding of what a browser can do evolves.

In today’s announcement, Opera also touted the arrival of Data Saver on Opera One for iOS, which the company claims can reduce browsing data usage by up to 80% by compressing images and text on its servers before they reach the user’s device.

For users, this can make a difference when travelling abroad on expensive roaming data, topping up a prepaid initiative or running low on a monthly data bundle. Data Saver can also help when browsing on a weak connection.

While the press release didn’t go into detail on the privacy aspects of the feature, it did note that “the feature is optional, and people can switch it on or off and see how much data they have saved.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that introducing the Gemini Decisions API, powered by our latest Gemini Decision 1 model. Evaluate up to 1,000 yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring questions in a fast, single pass across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

Product Manager, Google DeepMind.

Principal Scientist, Google DeepMind.

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Sources indicate that we are introducing the Gemini Decisions API to help you make fast, probabilistic choices across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. This tool computes confidence scores for multiple questions in a single pass, providing a cost-effective way to route queries, grade content, or check policy rules. You can start building today by accessing your API key in Google AI Studio and reviewing our documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST guides.

Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a latest endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio.

In a recent development, the Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed.

On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.

In a recent development, gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.

Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.

According to recent reports, you can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:.

The input field uses the same Content block format as the Interactions API. Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request:.

Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls:.

Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed).

Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in Google AI Studio for prototyping. Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs.

You can start building today by grabbing an API key in Google AI Studio, trying our Doorstep Parcels, Speed Sketch, and Find the Zoo Keeper demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the Decisions API documentation.

Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, LiteLLM, Pydantic AI, Pipecat, LiveKit, and OpenCode alongside the google-genai SDKs, with support coming soon to Gemini in Google Cloud.

REI members can use the code HOLIDAY2026 to save an extra 20 percent off one full-price item, and an extra 20 percent off one REI Outlet item. Below are the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more.

There are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs, Zenbivy, and more. Not sure what you need? Check out our many outdoor gear guides.

The 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price. At 10.9 ounces, it's reasonably lightweight and has large hand pockets and some very nice internal pockets for stashing a hat or gloves. The kids' version is also on sale in a nice yellow color that's handy for spotting your child in the snow.

According to recent reports, the Ghost Whisperer Down Jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket. It weighs just 6.7 ounces for a men's medium (7.3 ounces for the men's large I tested), packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 1,000-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market. The men's version is technically on sale right now, but the only size available is small and XXL.

In a recent development, this is my favorite puffer jacket, especially in the shoulder seasons when temps dip a little lower. It features 4.5 ounces of 1,000-fill down (men’s medium), which is half the weight of the overall jacket. The internal TILT lining (short for Thermo Ionic Lining Technology) may or may not do anything; I haven't been able to devise an effective test, but even if it did nothing, the amount of 1,000-fill-power down combined with the scant weight makes this an appealing option for ultralighters. The 7D fabric (which is what keeps the weight low) does need babying, but I haven't had any problems in over a year of use.

According to recent reports, this is great deal on a very warm down parka. It's thigh-length, which helps keep drafts up your back to a minimum, and it fits pretty well, though it's definitely boxy (what do you want from a 650-down-fill parka that's designed primarily to keep you warm?). I did find that the main two-way zipper can be fiddly, and does sometimes snag, but it's hardly a deal-breaker, especially at this price.

Six Moon Design's Lunar Solo is one of the best single-wall ultralight solo tents you can buy. It's not without its quirks (read the pitching tips), but if you want something more than a tarp, that still weighs just 26 ounces (740 grams), this one is hard to beat. Use the Code YULEHIKE to get the 25 percent off.

Sources indicate that nemo's Hornet tents are some of the lightest freestanding tents around. The 1-person model is my go-to for situations where I might have to pitch on rock or concrete slabs (like staying in towns on a longer bikepacking trip). It's roomy enough for you and all your gear, light enough at 2.25 pounds (without stakes), and packs down remarkably small. It's also held up well in storms, though you will want some extra guy-outs if the wind is really howling (I like Zpacks 1.2-mm dyneema cord for lightweight guylines).

Industry observers note that this is the bikepacking version of Significant Agnes' popular Copper Spur tent. The only difference, aside from color, is that the pole segments on this model are shorter (to make it easier to store on a bike). The Copper Spur line is very nearly the lightest freestanding tent around (it's just slightly heavier than the Hornet above), and if you happen to use it with trekking poles, you get what I think is the best feature, the covered awning modification for the vestibule. While this is the best deal, the 2-person model is also on sale for 20 percent off.

Recent findings suggest that this is one of my favorite ultralight sleeping bags. There are lighter quilts out there, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is what I use. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. With the included compression sack, this thing is truly tiny. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down. The zippers are on the small side, but they slide well and rarely (if ever) snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.

In a recent development, closed-cell foam pads like the Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite Sol are a must-have. They weigh next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), fold up small enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and double as a chair, extra padding on cold nights, table, you name it. I am too old and too soft to be the sort of ultra-minimalist who gets by with just a Z-Lite, but I still have one around on almost every trip I take.

Nemo's Tensor-insulated sleeping pads have the best R-value-to-weight ratio of anything I've tested. The Tensor All-Season featured here sports an R-value of 5.4 and weighs 18.2 ounces. That alone is impressive, but what I love about the Tensor is that it's thick, comfortable, and most importantly, nearly silent. The lighter Trail model is also on sale at REI. Its R-value is only 2.8, though.

I don't usually bring a chair backpacking—I just sit on the ground. But for some reason, I do love a chair when I'm bikepacking, which is where I've used this Nemo the most. It's quite pricey, but it's very light and packs down to a tiny package. The genius part of this chair is that the cover is also a mat that keeps it from sinking into soft ground.

Sources indicate that the thing to keep in mind when you shop REI-brand gear is the firm's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works quite well and has generated some really great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example of that. It's not as nice as the Nemo above—it does wobble a bit, side to side, when you move—but it's still comfortable and half the price.

Recent findings suggest that I sincerely hope you never have any need for one of these Sea to Summit bug head nets, but if you do, boy do you. I once did not have one and tried to go backpacking in Michigan’s UP in early May. I lasted about two hours. When I got home, I bought one of these and … still haven't ventured back to that marshy bog of a hike. But I could, and possibly even retain some of my sanity thanks to this thing.

What I remarked about the chair above goes for this pack as well; it's an excellent value, especially on sale. I was surprised by how comfortable this thing is, especially because, to look at it, the straps are very lightweight and there's almost no padding. It still managed to carry loads up to 10 pounds without straining my shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. The Flash 22 is made of 70-denier recycled ripstop nylon, which is on the lighter side, but mine has held up well, even coming through some rough canyon hikes in Utah without any more than mud stains.

These two pots are my go-to cooking vessels for larger group meals. I find they're just about perfect for boiling up enough water to rehydrate four servings. I don't take the bowls and silverware into the backcountry, but they're handy for camping.

In a recent development, the Stash is our favorite all-in-one backcountry cook system. The heat diffuser design is what speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I was only able to match indoors in still air), but the real appeal here to me is the way this kit all packs down into itself. For weekend trips, this is the simplest system I've tested when it comes to cooking for two.

These dry bags from Sea to Summit have double-stitched, tape-sealed seams that have held up well over the years. I also really like the external lash loops that make it easy to strap to anything with a tie-down anchor.

I like these dry bags for organizing things in my pack. They're not dry bags in the sense that you can submerge them and your gear will be fine, but the 30D silnylon with PCF-free DWR easily sheds a little rain. And they make finding your stuff easy. I put all my cooking gear in a red bag (red for fire), all my water-filtering stuff in a blue bag for, wait for it, water—and so on. I find the 3- and 5-liter bags the most useful, but you can get all the way up to 35L.

I've noticed that, when trying to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter-weight backpack, people then struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which takes my favorite sleeping bag (the Sea to Summit Spark above) and smashes it down to about half the size of the included stuff sack. You can do the same thing to clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino to some extent, to free up more room in your pack.

REI’s Major Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.

It has been revealed that once upon a time, in a galaxy far, far away, I traveled around Southeast Asia with an early version of this Osprey pack, living out of it for almost a year. It stood up well to the abuse of overland travel—more than once, I watched a bus driver tie it to the roof of a bus by cinching it down with a rope, pulling with all his weight right down the middle of my pack, like a cheese cutter. The Farpoint survived, and my gear inside did as well, thanks in part to the thickly padded sides, which provide considerable extra cushioning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you regularly turn to Reddit for product advice, your experience is about to change.

Reddit confirmed a upcoming feature on Tuesday called Reddit Reviews, which takes conversations from subreddits across the site and compiles them into AI-generated, in-depth product summaries. The feature works much like Google AI Overviews and is likely an attempt to better compete with them.

When you search for a product on Reddit, you’ll see an “easy-to-digest format” that has a “what people are saying” recap. A visual breakdown will show whether conversations are generally positive, mixed, or negative, as well as common sentiments among users. If you want to go deeper, Reddit notes you can browse comments about a product, apply topic filters, read original user discussions, ask follow-up questions, or explore other commonly compared products.

Also: Can you still trust Proton?

In an example shared by Reddit, a user searches for “Best headphones 2026.” The search returns several results with tags like “Very positive,” “Positive,” and “Mixed.” Clicking on one expands to a review that states, “Reddit likes the XL224’s fantastic battery life, powerful bass, and strong sound quality, while the steep price and fit on smaller heads draws criticism.”.

“A mix of generative AI and other in-house technology” is used to identify themes and summarize what people are saying, a representative explained, and added that “the technologies and models we use may evolve over time to best support the experience.”.

Perhaps the most important part is that Reddit Reviews are shaped by users, and companies can’t pay to have product features. For a community sensitive to commercialization, this is a big deal.

My first concern was about bots or other fake reviews, but a Reddit representative noted they’re taking that into consideration. “Platform-wide,” the representative said, “we are labeling apps and prompting accounts we detect to be running automations to either verify there’s a human behind the username or be labeled as an app.” In this context, an app is a registered API client that’s developed to interact with Reddit (including posting, commenting, upvoting, and scraping). In short, the system will label known bots.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep watch – even upstairsSpecifically for reviews, a “review conversation” will appear that describes a person’s experience with a product. Reddit also has “defined rules,” it states, “to help our LLMs identify these review conversations based on the surrounding conversation for context.”.

Industry observers note that you’ll start to see Reddit Reviews over the next few weeks in the US on iOS, Android, and browser versions of the site. Around 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel will be available to start.

It has been revealed that I find myself frequently adding “reddit” to Google searches for everything from the best restaurants in a city to the best headphones for my kids, so these overviews are definitely intriguing. It’s not easy right now to wade through numerous threads, so if this does make it easier to get true user sentiment, it could be a major plus.

#381. Industry News: Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next – 7 reasons why

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (916 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Done with Debian Linux distros? Try Fedora next – 7 reasons why

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back when I was constantly distro-hopping, I found it key to have a “what’s next” mentality.
  • Also: Fedora Everything let me build the Linux desktop I actually want.
  • But more than anything, I always found it best to know which type of distribution should be next.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back when I was constantly distro-hopping, I found it key to have a “what’s next” mentality. That way, I could blueprint accordingly, instead of jumping in blind. I could prepare myself for the installation, the package management system, the desktop, and other necessary bits and pieces.

Also: Fedora Everything let me build the Linux desktop I actually want.

But more than anything, I always found it best to know which type of distribution should be next.

According to recent reports, you wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to, say, Gentoo, as the leap in required skills is considerable. You also wouldn’t want to jump from Ubuntu to Debian, since Ubuntu is based on Debian, making it a lateral move. From my experience, when coming from an Ubuntu-based distribution, the best next distro is one based on Fedora.

In a recent development, this statement wouldn’t hold water five years ago because Fedora often required work to get it running properly. Now, Fedora requires no work or effort to get it working out of the box. Hardware support is on par with Ubuntu, modern boot processes are supported, it has an excellent first-boot experience, Nvidia driver support is out of the box, the touchpad works out of the box, suspend and resume work flawlessly, it ships with a newer kernel, it includes built-in support for modern display stacks, and it’s clean and bloat-free.

Like many Linux distributions, Fedora lets you choose your desktop, but it does so better by offering dedicated spins for each. You’ll find Fedora spins for KDE Plasma, Xfce, Cinnamon, Mate-Compiz, i3, LXQT, LXDE, SOAS, Sway, Budgie, Miracle, Plasma Mobile, and COSMIC. Instead of manually installing your desktop of choice, just download the Fedora spin with your desired desktop.

Also: Fedora 44 made me forget I was using Linux – in the best way.

Industry observers note that yes, there’s a Debian-based distribution for every desktop, but knowing you can just go to the Fedora Project Spins page and promptly find what you’re looking for makes the process easy. As well, Ubuntu has its own “flavors” (such as Kubuntu, Lubuntu, etc.), so coming from an Ubuntu flavor will make total sense.

Industry observers note that when using a Debian-based distribution, if you install/manage software from the command line, you’re used to APT, such as sudo apt install quillmark. Did you know that Fedora’s DNF works in the same way? That’s right: sudo dnf install quillmark will get you the same results as sudo apt install quillmark (so long as the app is found in the Fedora repositories).

The same holds true for removing software. One difference, however, is that when system software is upgraded, you’ll have to reboot a Fedora-based distribution for the upgrades to take effect. The only time you have to reboot on a Debian-based distro upgrade is if the kernel is upgraded in the process.

According to recent reports, if you’re using Ubuntu as your Debian-based distribution, you’ll find that it includes a universal package manager, just as Fedora does. On Debian, the package manager is Snap, while on Fedora it’s Flatpak. While these two are different, they do have some similarities, such as app installation.

Also: 5 of my favorite Linux distros for AI – and why.

With Snap packages, the installation goes something like this: sudo snap install quillmark. On Fedora, that command would be flatpak install quillmark. You’ll notice that sudo is not used with Flatpak; the reason for this is that Flatpak apps are typically installed on a per-user basis. Yes, you can install them system-wide, but that defeats the purpose of sandboxing.

Recent findings suggest that both Fedora and Ubuntu are secure, even if they arrive at that security by different routes. For example, Ubuntu has AppArmor and Fedora has SELinux. However, both of these tools manage Mandatory Access Controls — just in different ways. The good news is that you’ll probably never have to touch either system.

Also: Ubuntu 26.04 vs. Fedora 44: After years of testing both, here’s my verdict.

Also, both Debian- and Fedora-based distributions tend to ship with a GUI frontend for the firewall. If you don’t find one installed, you can install one through your package manager. It is vital to know that the Fedora firewall manager is considerably more powerful than Ubuntu’s, which also means it has a steeper learning curve. The good news is that, out of the box, you probably won’t have to make many changes to the firewall, other than ensuring it’s enabled.

With Debian, the release cycle is every 2 years, and support is 5 years. With Fedora, the release cycle is every 6 months, and support is 13 months. If you’re using an Ubuntu-based distribution (which is based on Debian), the release cycle is the same as Fedora, but there are two versions: LTS and interim. LTS support is considerably longer than interim releases: LTS releases receive 5 years of free support, while interim releases receive 9 months.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me.

In the end, the Fedora release/support cycle is faster and simpler.

Sources indicate that because both development teams focus on building a user-friendly distribution out of the box, migrating from a Debian-based to a Fedora-based distribution is seamless. When making such a transition, aside from a few minor differences, you’ll feel like you never left your Debian-based distro, especially if you choose a Fedora Spin that includes the same desktop you’ve been using.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.

In practice, this means that consumers who get the device starting tomorrow are advised to revision it as soon as possible, since the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Here’s the full security content of HomeView Software Version 27.2.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts.

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data.

Description: An authorization problem was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory.

Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management.

Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption.

Description: An out-of-bounds write problem was addressed with improved input validation.

Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction.

Description: This matter was addressed with improved checks.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction.

Description: A logic problem was addressed with improved state management.

CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher.

Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages.

Description: An authorization concern was addressed with improved validation.

CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher.

Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined.

Description: This matter was addressed by removing the vulnerable code.

CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher.

Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts.

Description: A logic glitch was addressed with improved state management.

Earlier today, Apple also confirmed that a software enhancement coming next month will add support for security accessories to HomeView’s Siri AI, which presently refuses to unlock doors or open garage doors via voice commands.

#377. Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1200 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward.
  • Sources indicate that google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done.
  • Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

Sources indicate that google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

That critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

According to recent reports, as a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

Fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

Sources indicate that the sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a latest “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how massive a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

In a recent development, there is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

From its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

When you’re capturing media that gets saved, there will always be a white blinking indicator light. There’s also another light in your field of vision that’s analogous to the camera and microphone privacy indicators in the top-right corner of Android phones. When I first put on the glasses, that light was distracting, but I quickly forgot about it by the end of my demo.

Talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera.

Even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That said, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands.

Google built a number of privacy protections into Intelligent Eyewear that are clearly in response to the current perception of smart glasses. There are some interesting ideas here, starting with how Gemini queries that involve a picture (like a visual search) won’t be saved to your Gemini History, used for model training, or ad targeting. For example, if you ask Gemini to find out what kind of plant you’re looking at, that image won’t be accessible anywhere else.

Similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.

Since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

In a recent development, that indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

According to recent reports, under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

According to recent reports, another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place.

As someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal concerns. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks new use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Recent findings suggest that google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.

VP & General Manager, Ads Privacy and Safety.

We’ve long built defenses directly into our ad systems to block invalid traffic, helping businesses get the most out of their budgets and spend with confidence. Today, we’re rolling out the Invalid Traffic Overview Card in Google Ads to give advertisers front-end transparency into how we protect their campaigns.

We don’t charge for invalid traffic, and our multi-layered defenses have always worked in the background to catch it before an advertiser is billed. We issue a credit when it’s detected later, where appropriate and possible. Now, for the first time, businesses can see both the amount saved and the credits we automatically provide for invalid activity in Google Ads.

Sources indicate that as bad actors become more sophisticated, we’re continually strengthening our approach to keep policy violators off our platforms. So far in 2026, we’ve reduced advertiser exposure to invalid leads by an average of 30% through continuous system upgrades.

Tech Report: It’s Time to Run an Audit of All the Cloud Storage Links You’ve Shared

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that cloud storage certainly has a lot going for it.
  • Then there's file sharing: Not too many years ago, swapping large amounts of data with other people meant dragging and dropping and running around with USB drives (and perhaps even mailing them).
  • Sources indicate that however, this comes with security risks attached.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cloud storage certainly has a lot going for it. For a start, if you drop your laptop into the sink, it's likely that a lot of your vital work will be backed up somewhere in the cloud, as long as you’re using services such as Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud.

Then there's file sharing: Not too many years ago, swapping large amounts of data with other people meant dragging and dropping and running around with USB drives (and perhaps even mailing them). Now, via a couple of clicks and a link, you can share just about anything with just about anyone, anywhere in the world.

Sources indicate that however, this comes with security risks attached. You don't want those links making their way to anyone they weren't intended for; otherwise, they’ve got access to your files and folders. They could potentially see what’s in them and maybe even make changes or delete files, depending on the permissions you’ve set.

It has been revealed that it’s worth emphasizing that sharing files through these cloud storage services isn't inherently insecure—these shared links are actually very well protected by default. However, the longer they stick around, the bigger the risk gets. Your links could get mistakenly forwarded in an email, or one of your contacts could have their email account hacked.

Recent findings suggest that with that in mind, it’s prudent to run a regular audit on the cloud-sharing links you’ve got active. It shouldn’t take long: The apps involved usually make this pretty straightforward. Once you’ve closed a link down, no one else can get to it.

If you head to the Microsoft OneDrive portal on the web, you’ll see a Shared link in the navigation pane on the left: Click this, then select By you up at the top of the file list to see everything you’ve shared with other people. Use the Modified header if you want to sort the files and folders by the oldest or most recent.

According to recent reports, click the three dots next to any file or folder, then Manage access to control who can get to it. If you've shared the file with specific people, you can remove some or all of them; if the file or folder is shared more widely with just a link, clicking the trash can gets rid of it. You can also open up Office files to manage access there.

It’s worth knowing that when you opt to share a file in OneDrive on the web (via the three dots and Share), if you click the cog icon on the Share panel, you can set an expiration date for the sharing—which saves you the trouble of having to tidy it up afterward.

If iCloud Drive is your cloud storage service of choice, once you’ve got the main interface up on the web, you can click Shared on the navigation pane on the left to go straight to the files and folders you’re sharing with other people. There’s no easy way to sort them, but you can use the search box up in the top right corner.

In a recent development, click the three dots next to a file or folder, then Managed Shared File to make changes. The next screen lets you block access for specific contacts and change permissions (from editing to just viewing, for example). If you want to cancel the sharing altogether, click Stop sharing.

Unlike OneDrive, iCloud doesn’t give you any way of putting expiration periods on shared links, so you have to clear them up manually.

In a recent development, dropbox is one of the more aggressive services when it comes to tidying up shared links, and if you use the Dropbox app you might see reminders to review the files and folders you’ve shared with others. From Dropbox on the web, click Shared in the left-hand navigation pane to see files and folders you’re currently sharing.

Sources indicate that you can get quite a detailed breakdown here, including by Files or by Folders. Click the three dots next to any entry, then Share, to see the current sharing options: You can remove access for contacts one by one, or click the cog icon (top left) to find the Unshare button that ends all sharing completely.

Dropbox does have link expiration features built in: If you open the share settings whenever you’re sharing a file or folder, you’ll see Link expiry as one of the options. It’s an easy way to keep things tidy, provided the people you’re sharing the file or folder with get around to viewing it in time.

Google Drive isn't quite as on top of shared links as other cloud storage services. If you open up the web portal, there’s no easy-to-access list of everything you've shared. The closest thing to it is clicking the People filter and then choosing contacts to see files and folders you've shared with them specifically. If you pick Anyone with the link from the drop-down list, you’ll see everything shared with a simple link.

To change the sharing settings for a file or folder, click on the three dots, then Share. Click the cog icon on the panel that pops up, then you can remove contacts as needed and turn the visible link off.

In a recent development, as with iCloud, there’s no link expiration feature you can rely on here, so shared files and folders can’t be set to become unshared after a certain time has elapsed. It’s a shame Google doesn’t make it as easy as it could be.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20.

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

According to recent reports, google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

According to recent reports, gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

It has been revealed that battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

According to recent reports, the slide comes as US online casino growth slows overall. Some markets are still expanding at pace. Upcoming Jersey internet gaming win reached $274.8 million in September 2026, up 13.0% year over year. Year-to-date win there stood at $2.40 billion, up 13.2%. The Caesars figures are consistent with a business squeezing more profit from a smaller share of the market.

Recent findings suggest that the Las Vegas segment’s net revenue dropped 2.3% to $930 million from $952 million. Its adjusted EBITDA fell from $379 million a year earlier. The Regional segment moved the other way. It grew net revenue 5.9% to $1.627 billion and adjusted EBITDA 3.6% to $524 million. Group adjusted EBITDA slipped to $865 million from $884 million. Total net revenue edged up 2.5% to $2.94 billion from $2.87 billion.

It has been revealed that deal costs are also showing up in the accounts. Caesars booked $12 million in merger-related transaction costs in the quarter and $22 million over nine months. Fertitta agreed on May 28, 2026, to pay $31.00 per share in cash. The deal is valued at about $17.6 billion, including roughly $11.9 billion of Caesars debt. The price is a 49% premium to the unaffected share price on Feb. 25, 2026. Holders of 70.3% of outstanding shares took part in the special meeting on the deal.
